messages.subject: Convergence issues on BSEM with deterministic missingness
messages.subject_clean: Convergence issues on BSEM with deterministic missingness
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I’m a beginner to Bayesian latent variable modeling, and I’ve been trying to use blavaan for a research project. Currently, as a proof of concept, I’m fitting a linear-Gaussian SEM on a synthetic dataset, where we have two features X_1 and X_2, one latent variable C, and two outcome variables D and Y. The values for the dataset are generated from a given SEM.

One really important point to note is that there is deterministic missingness in Y: if the value of D is 0 in the dataset, then Y is missing. (But D has no other direct effect on Y.) Currently, I am using the default FIML method to handle missingness, but perhaps FIML isn’t built for this situation?

The following plot is the SEM that I’m trying to estimate.

Below are plots of the values in this synthetic dataset, with the points’ position given by X, and colored by D in the first plot, and Y in the second. (Note that due to deterministic missingness, all the points in the graph colored by Y come from the subset of points where D = 1.)

The point is: the model takes longer than I believe it should to converge, often using over 10,000 iterations to converge (per the blavaan documentation, “If your model is not converging after 1,000 burnin samples, it is likely that the default prior distributions clash with your data.”) I’ve tried tightening the priors, and while that hasn’t improved convergence, I haven’t messed with the priors in any very structured way, so perhaps that is still the solution.

I was hoping someone could advise me on whether I’m making any mistakes using the package, or whether this is just inherent to the problem I'm trying to specify. The following is the model I’m using to specify the model, and the code I’m running to estimate it in blavaan.

# import dataset
data <- read.csv('data/dataset_current.csv', header = TRUE)

# create lavaan model
model <- '
  C =~ NA*X_1 + X_2 + D + Y
  D ~ X_1 + X_2

  # everything has variance
  C ~~ C
  D ~~ D
  Y ~~ Y
  X_1 ~~ X_1
  X_2 ~~ X_2

  # correlations between features
  X_1 ~~ X_2

  # and everything has an intercept
  C ~ 1
  D ~ 1
  Y ~ 1
  X_1 ~ 1
  X_2 ~ 1
'

BURN <- 1000
rhat <- 20
while(rhat > 1.01) {
  BURN <- BURN + 1000
  fit_continuous <- bsem(model, data = data, n.chains = 4, sample = 1000, burnin = BURN, bcontrol = list(cores = 4), mcmcfile = TRUE, save.lvs = TRUE)
  rhat <- max(blavInspect(fit_continuous, "psrf"), na.rm = TRUE)
  print(paste0("Rhat=", rhat))
}

Thank you in advance for your help, and for the work and support y'all provide in creating and maintaining a solution like blavaan!

could you show the summary() of your model? I think you might have an unidentified model because you relaease the constraint on the first factor loading ( C =~ NA*X_1 + X_2 + D + Y ), but didnt add any other identification method. Try adding the argument std.lv <http://std.lv>=T to the bsem function to identofy it by fixing the latent variance to 1

If that still doesnt work, we can look at using the priors to constraint the parameter space.

About the missing structucture. These missing patterns are notoriously problemaic. If you use the default FIMCMC (full information MCMC, is what I call the approach used in blavaan as it is similar to FIML but is not ML) would estimate the model as if everyone had answer everything to estimate the parameters. But would lead to interpretatibility issues

messages.body_plain:
I am not sure that the missingness thing is the major problem. I think the parameters of this model are not identified, beyond std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE or FALSE. All the observed variables are connected by regression relationships (directed paths), and also by the latent variable C. So I think that the regression parameters will trade off with the loadings (the paths coming off C), which would explain why the model is not converging.

This is a place where lavaan can really help, because it will quickly tell you something is wrong in the maximum likelihood version of the model. Just do

library("lavaan")
sem(model, data = data)

For this model, I believe lavaan will report negative degrees of freedom and also report that it can't invert the information matrix. I think this means that you need to either eliminate free parameters or constrain some parameters to be equal. Mauricio also mentioned using informative priors to try to constrain the parameters to an identified posterior distribution, which may be possible but I think also tricky.

Best,
Ed

With 4 variables, you have 10 unique elements of the coavriance matrix, and have 11 parameters (means dont count in this). So, need to remove at least 1 parameter

Also, another problem is that even with std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, the mean on C is being estimated because you wrote it in the sytnax, instead of being fixed to 0. Now, it might be that having the variables have direct relations, and relations through the latent variable could make the model hard to find a solution

I would simplify the syntax like this, and rely on the defaults to estimate the variances (by default) and the means (meanstructure=T).

You can indeed specify constraints for target = "jags". You would use the "==" operator, which is also available in lavaan. Continuing with the previous example:

m1 <- ' visual =~ x1 + prior("dnorm(hmu,.5)")*x2 + load1*x2 + load2*x3
        load2 == load1^2 '

fit <- bcfa(m1, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, target = "jags",

            mcmcextra = list(syntax = "hmu ~ dnorm(0, .0001)",
                             monitor = "hmu"))

And when you use "==" in blavaan, you can only have one parameter on the left of ==. So a constraint like

load1 + load2 == load3 + load4

needs to become

load1 == load3 + load4 - load2

That is a little more restrictive than lavaan, which will accept more complex arguments on the lhs.

messages.body_plain:
Niels,

I would be interested to see the error message from Stan on this one.

It looks like your model has no latent variables, so that convergence problems are not due to sign indeterminacy issues. I would then guess that the default priors in blavaan clash with your observed data. Especially if you have variables that take values far from 0, this can cause problems. Maybe the best thing to do is specify your own priors that are tailored to your model and data. A fast thing to do is standardize all your variables to see whether that aids in convergence.

Ed

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I believe that in Stan, a comparison of models using LOO is based on the expected log predictive density under leave-one-out (ELPD_loo) along with a standard error for comparison.  In other words, the difference that is formed is the difference in ELPD_loo values for each model.  In blavaan, what is reported is the difference in LOO values that can be compared to the standard error.  This seems to be a difference in the LOOICs for each model which would be the differences in -2*ELPD_(loo) for each model.   What is actually being reported by blavCompare and if it is the difference in LOOICs, then how is the standard error being calculated?

https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html

Thanks in advance,

David

David

This is a labeling issue, the "LOO difference and & SE" section of blavCompare reports the difference in ELPD_loo and the respective SE. But we report the LOOIC estimates as people are more commonly use to the IC metric instead of the ELPD, for interpretability and direction of the differences.
